{{cite web |title=Wilmar International Limited,「丰益国际」 |url=https://www.kuokgroup.com/cn/businesses/wilmar |website=The Kuok Group |access-date=13 September 2020 |archive-date=9 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220309215002/https://www.kuokgroup.com/cn/businesses/wilmar |url-status=live }} is a [[Singapore]]an [[food processing]] and [[investment]] [[holding company]] with more than 300 [[subsidiary]] companies.{{Cite web |url=https://www.wilmar-international.com/annualreport2020/pdf/Wilmar-International-AR2020.pdf |title=Annual Report 2020 |publisher=Wilmar International |access-date=16 October 2021}}{{rp|18}} Founded in 1991, it is one of Asia's leading [[agribusiness]] groups alongside the [[COFCO Group]]. It ranks amongst the largest listed companies by market capitalisation on the [[Singapore Exchange]] (SGX), being the second largest as of September 2010.{{cite news | url=https://www.forbes.com/global/2010/0809/singapore-10-40-richest-kuok-khoon-hong-wilmar-harvest.html | work=[[Forbes.com]] | title=Wilmar's Harvest | date=9 August 2010 | archive-date=5 December 2016 | access-date=18 September 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161205121447/http://www.forbes.com/global/2010/0809/singapore-10-40-richest-kuok-khoon-hong-wilmar-harvest.html | url-status=live }} It was ranked 211th in the [[Fortune Global 500]] list in 2020.{{cite web|url=http://fortune.com/global500/wilmar-international/ |title=Fortune Global 500 |url-access=subscription |access-date=16 October 2021}} It was ranked 3rd in the World's Most Admired Company (Food Production) by ''[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]'' in 2019.{{cite web|url=http://fortune.com/worlds-most-admired-companies/wilmar-international/ |title=Fortune World's Most Admired Companies |url-access=subscription |access-date=30 May 2019}} Wilmar International business activities include [[oil palm]] cultivation, [[edible oil]]s refining, oilseeds crushing, consumer pack edible oils processing and merchandising, specialty fats, [[oleochemicals]], and [[biodiesel]] manufacturing, grains processing and merchandising, and sugar milling and refining. In 2021, Wilmar placed 2nd on FoodTalks' Global Top 30 Specialty Oil Companies list.{{Cite web|last=Fu|first=Rice|date=2021-05-26|title=2021年全球特种油脂企业30强|url=https://www.foodtalks.cn/news/foodnews/top_100/6037|access-date=2022-01-24|website=FoodTalks|language=zh|archive-date=21 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220121105731/https://www.foodtalks.cn/news/foodnews/top_100/6037|url-status=live}} It has over 500 manufacturing plants and an extensive distribution network covering [[China]], [[Indonesia]], [[India]] and some 50 other countries. The group employs a multinational workforce of more than 100,000 people.{{rp|28}} Wilmar's merchandising and processing segment encompasses merchandising of [[#Palm oil|palm oil]] and [[laurics]]-related products, operations of palm oil processing and [[Refining|refinery]] plants and crushing, further processing and refining of a range of edible oils, [[oilseed]]s, [[grain]]s and [[soybean]]. Its consumer products include edible oils, rice, flour and noodles in China, Indonesia, [[Vietnam]] and India. Its plantation and palm oil mills segment engages in oil palm [[Plant cultivation|cultivation]] and [[Mill (grinding)|milling]]. Wilmar has come under criticism for its exploitation of [[child labour]] and [[Forced labour|slave labour]], as well as unsafe working conditions on its plantations amidst other worker mistreatment incidents. The company has also been exposed for its environmentally degrading practices, and [[forced displacement]] of poor populations, amongst other unethical behaviours. Wilmar was ranked fourth within the global food production sector in Fortune's most admired firms list in 2026.{{Cite web |last=Lim |first=Chloe |date=2026-01-22 |title=SIA, Wilmar the only Singapore companies to make Fortune’s most admired firms list |url=https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/companies-markets/sia-wilmar-only-singapore-companies-make-fortunes-most-admired-firms-list |access-date=2026-01-23 |website=The Business Times |language=en}} ==History== Wilmar was founded by [[Kuok Khoon Hong]] and [[Martua Sitorus]] on 1 April, 1991{{Cite web |url=https://www.wilmar-international.com/about-us/history-milestones |title=History & Milestones |access-date=16 October 2021 |publisher=Wilmar International}} and commenced operations as a palm oil trading company. profile== [[Unilever]] is one of the main customers of Wilmar. Unilever and Wilmar are members of the [[Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil]] (RSPO) which brings together retailers, producers and [[NGOs]] like [[Oxfam]] and [[World Wide Fund for Nature|WWF]].{{Cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/6927890.stm |title=Losing land to palm oil in Kalimantan |publisher=BBC News |last=Painter |first=James |date=3 August 2007 |access-date=16 October 2021 |archive-date=8 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180108065031/http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/6927890.stm |url-status=live }} ==Palm oil== [[Palm oil]], extracted from [[palm fruit]] pulp, is Wilmar's main product. Palm oil is the most widely used edible oil, and there are 42 million acres under cultivation worldwide. Commercial production has helped many communities in Africa and South-east Asia tackle local poverty. However, environmentalists have been concerned that such widespread cultivation has led to [[deforestation]] and [[air pollution]], and is a threat to [[endangered species]]. In 2013, Wilmar changed its approach and endorsed [[sustainability]] principles. As a part of this it sold its subsidiary [[PT Asiatic Persada]] which for its involvement in land grabs.{{cite web |url=http://www.iht.com/2014/05/05/the-dirty-business-of-palm-oil/ |title=The Dirty Business of Palm Oil {{!}} International Herald Tribune |website=www.iht.com |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715002405/http://www.iht.com/2014/05/05/the-dirty-business-of-palm-oil/ |archive-date=2014-07-15}} ==Ethical issues== In 2004, [[Friends of the Earth Europe|Friends of the Earth Netherlands]] performed a review of Wilmar's palm oil operations in [[Sumatra]] Riau as undertaken by PT Jatim Jaya Perkasa. Wilmar had 20,800 hectares of land there and the operation was financed by the Dutch [[Rabobank]] and the [[International Finance Corporation]]. Satellite photos proved that in 2004, the plantations were on sea shore [[peat]] [[rain forests]], the depth of the peat being four meters, whereas such land is actually protected under Indonesian law. Nevertheless, in 1997 Wilmar received permission to plant there despite it being peat land. According to locals, the plantation endangers the [[Sumatran tiger]] population that inhabits the area, and this became a point of conflict with Wilmar in 2004. Soon after, Wilmar sold PT Jatim Jaya Perkasa and joined the [[World Wide Fund for Nature|WWF]] Palm Oil Association.{{Citation needed|date=June 2023}} According to Friends of the Earth Netherlands, Wilmar International starts [[forest fire]]s and violates the rights of local populations.{{cite web|url=http://www.foeeurope.org/press/2007/July3_PDC_Wilmar_PalmOil.htm |title=World's biggest palm oil trader shamed | Friends of the Earth Europe | Company involved in forest fires, deforestation and illegal activities |publisher=foeeurope.org|access-date=30 May 2016|archivedate=April 30, 2022|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220430122358/https://friendsoftheearth.eu/press-release/worlds-biggest-palm-oil-trader-shamed/}} In July 2007, [[Friends of the Earth]] and two local environmental organizations criticized Wilmar's [[illegal logging|illegal forest felling]] in [[Kalimantan]], in Indonesia. As a result of this campaign against Wilmar's projects in [[Sambas Regency|Sambas]], [[West Kalimantan]], the company agreed to implement a number of new measures and policies.{{cite archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905224421/http://www.foei.org/press/archive-by-subject/food-sovereignty-press/ugandan-oil-palm-conglomerate-taken-court-land-grab-claims| url-status=dead}} According to [[The Guardian]] in March 2015, the land grab issue has plagued the community of Kalangala for a number of years. In July 2011, residents awoke to "find yellow machines churning up her land and razing the crops she had grown in a bid to make way for palm oil plantations."{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2015/mar/03/ugandan-farmers-take-on-palm-oil-giants-over-land-grab-claims| title=Ugandan farmers take on palm oil giants over land grab claims|first=Alon |last=Mwesigwa|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|date=3 March 2015|access-date=26 February 2016}} [[Bidco Africa]] and Wilmar have made no recorded statement on these matters. Again according to [[Friends of the Earth International]], the projects implications include: Forced displacement, poor labour standards, deforestation, and insecurity amongst other.{{cite web|url=http://libcloud.s3.amazonaws.com/93/7b/3/3078/Issue_Brief_5_-_Wilmar_in_Uganda.pdf|title=Palm oil landgrab in Uganda: Wilmar International's violations in Kalangala Island|access-date=26 February 2016|last=FOEI|publisher=Libcloud.s3.amazonaws.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304102200/http://libcloud.s3.amazonaws.com/93/7b/3/3078/Issue_Brief_5_-_Wilmar_in_Uganda.pdf|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead}} The community have now taken the conglomerate to court.{{cite AV media|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w21NJGbtBuQ |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/w21NJGbtBuQ |archive-date=21 December 2021 |url-status=live|title=The Land Grab – Uganda's farmers battle with palm oil producers|date=12 July 2015|work=YouTube}}{{cbignore}} In February 2016, the [[United Nations Development Programme]] (UNDP) received a petition from the Bugala Farmers Association in [[Uganda]] related to UNDP's association with Bidco Africa Ltd.{{Cite web|url=http://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/presscenter/pressreleases/2016/02/25/statement-concerning-undp-business-call-to-action-and-bidco-africa-ltd-.html|title=Statement concerning UNDP, Business Call to Action and Bidco Africa Ltd.|access-date=22 May 2017|archive-date=3 January 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170103084753/http://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/presscenter/pressreleases/2016/02/25/statement-concerning-undp-business-call-to-action-and-bidco-africa-ltd-.html/|url-status=dead}} A complaint was also received by the UNDP's Stakeholder Response Mechanism (SRM) and Social and Environmental Compliance Unit (SECU).{{Cite web|url=https://info.undp.org/sites/registry/secu/SECUPages/CaseDetail.aspx?ItemID=7|title=Social and Environmental Compliance Unit - Case Registry|website=info.undp.org}} In May 2016, [[UNDP]] visited Kalangala to further investigate the issues surrounding the matter.{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S0ifty2XUTw|title=UNDP to Investigate Rights Violations at BIDCO|last=NBS TV Uganda|date=29 May 2016|via=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}{{Dead Youtube links|date=February 2022}} In November 2016, the UNDP faulted a decision inviting Bidco Ltd into partnership with the United Nations Development Programme's Business Call to Action in Uganda.{{Cite web|title=Bidco is not fit to join UNDP's project – UN|url=https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2016/11/18/bidco-is-not-fi-t-to-join-undps-project-un_c1457644|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161119144140/https://www.the-star.co.ke/news/2016/11/18/bidco-is-not-fi-t-to-join-undps-project-un_c1457644|archive-date=19 November 2016|website=The Star}} === Human right violations in 2016 === On 30 November 2016, [[Amnesty International]] published a report into working conditions on the Wilmar International plantations and refineries in Indonesia. It alleged human rights abuses, including "forced labour, low pay, exposure to toxic chemicals and discrimination against women".{{cite web|title=Human rights abuses in your shopping basket|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2016/11/sustainable-palm-oil-abuse-exposed/|website=www.amnesty.org|date=30 November 2016|archivedate=April 30, 2022|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20220430121952/https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2016/11/sustainable-palm-oil-abuse-exposed/}} According to [[Amnesty International]], Wilmar International profited from 8- to 14-year-old child labour and forced labour. Some workers were extorted, threatened or not paid for work. Some workers suffered severe injuries from exposure to [[herbicide]]s containing [[paraquat]]. Wilmar customers include [[FAMSA]], [[Archer Daniels Midland|ADM]], [[Colgate-Palmolive]], [[Elevance]], [[Kellogg's]], [[Nestlé]], [[Procter & Gamble]], [[Reckitt Benckiser]] and [[Unilever]]. Wilmar palm oil may be used in popular products like [[Magnum (ice cream)|Magnum]] ice-cream, [[Colgate (toothpaste)|Colgate]] toothpaste, [[Dove (toiletries)]], [[Knorr (brand)|Knorr]] soup, [[KitKat]], [[Pantene]] shampoo, [[Ariel (detergent)|Ariel]], and [[Pot Noodle]].[https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/asa21/5184/2016/en/ THE GREAT PALM OIL SCANDAL: LABOUR ABUSES BEHIND BIG BRAND NAMES] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180423210624/https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/asa21/5184/2016/en/ |date=23 April 2018 }} Amnesty International 30 November 2016 ===NDPE Initiatives=== On 5 December 2013, Wilmar committed to a No Deforestation, No Peat & No Exploitation Policy (NDPE policy){{Cite web |url=http://www.wilmar-international.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/11/No-Deforestation-No-Peat-No-Exploitation-Policy.pdf |title=No Deforestation, No Peat & No Exploitation Policy |date=5 December 2013 |publisher=Wilmar International |access-date=16 October 2021}} for both its own operations and third party suppliers.{{cite web |date=5 December 2013 |url=http://www.climateadvisers.com/tft-and-climate-advisers-welcome-wilmars-transformative-policies-to-protect-forests-and-people/ |title=TFT and Climate Advisers Welcome Wilmar's Transformative Policies to Protect Forests and People | Climate Advisers |publisher=Climate Advisers |website=climateadvisers.com |access-date=30 May 2016}} It promised to stop buying from suppliers who cleared forest, drained peat land, or exploited locals.{{cite web |url=http://grist.org/food/48-hours-that-changed-the-future-of-rainforests/ |last=Johnson |first=Nathanael |date=2 April 2015 |title=48 hours that changed the future of rainforests |publisher=Grist Magazine, Inc. |website=grist.org |access-date=30 May 2016 |archive-date=26 May 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160526191728/http://grist.org/food/48-hours-that-changed-the-future-of-rainforests/ |url-status=live }} This was lauded as a transformational step towards responsible and sustainable palm oil development.{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sustainable-business/wilmar-no-deforestation-commitment-food-production |title=Wilmar's 'no deforestation' commitment could revolutionise the way food is grown |last=Poynton |first=Scott |newspaper=The Guardian |date=29 January 2014 |access-date=30 May 2016}} Preliminary analysis estimated that Wilmar's commitment would eliminate more than 1.5Gt CO2 emissions in total between 2016 and 2020. === Recognition / Awards === In 2015, Wilmar won the Special Recognition Award at the Singapore Apex CSR Awards 2015 organised by the Global Compact Network Singapore, [[Singapore Business Federation]] and [[The Business Times (Singapore)|The Business Times]]. It was hailed for being the first major palm oil player to step up to ensure its supply chain is de-linked from any forest destruction and human rights abuse.{{cite web|url=http://www.eco-business.com/news/singapore-businesses-mark-10-years-of-csr-push/|title=Singapore businesses mark 10 years of CSR push | News | Eco-Business | Asia Pacific|publisher=eco-business.com|access-date=30 May 2016|archive-date=7 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160807152106/http://www.eco-business.com/news/singapore-businesses-mark-10-years-of-csr-push/|url-status=live}} == References == {{Reflist|30em}} ==External links== * [official website] {{FTSE STI constituents}} {{DJSI World}} {{Palm oil}} {{Authority control}} [[Category:Agriculture companies of Singapore]] [[Category:Companies listed on the Singapore Exchange]] [[Category:Companies in the Straits Times Index]] [[Category:Multinational companies headquartered in Singapore]] [[Category:Palm oil production in Indonesia]] [[Category:Palm oil production in Malaysia]] [[Category:Palm oil production in Nigeria]] [[Category:Agriculture companies established in the 1990s]] [[Category:Companies established in 1991]] [[Category:Singaporean brands]]

Wilmar International Limited (simplified Chinese: 丰益国际; traditional Chinese: 豐益國際; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: Hong-ek Kok-chè) is a Singaporean food processing and investment holding company with more than 300 subsidiary companies. Founded in 1991, it is one of Asia's leading agribusiness groups alongside the COFCO Group. It ranks amongst the largest listed companies by market capitalisation on the Singapore Exchange (SGX), being the second largest as of September 2010. It was ranked 211th in the Fortune Global 500 list in 2020. It was ranked 3rd in the World's Most Admired Company (Food Production) by Fortune in 2019.
Wilmar International business activities include oil palm cultivation, edible oils refining, oilseeds crushing, consumer pack edible oils processing and merchandising, specialty fats, oleochemicals, and biodiesel manufacturing, grains processing and merchandising, and sugar milling and refining. In 2021, Wilmar placed 2nd on FoodTalks' Global Top 30 Specialty Oil Companies list. It has over 500 manufacturing plants and an extensive distribution network covering China, Indonesia, India and some 50 other countries. The group employs a multinational workforce of more than 100,000 people.
Wilmar's merchandising and processing segment encompasses merchandising of palm oil and laurics-related products, operations of palm oil processing and refinery plants and crushing, further processing and refining of a range of edible oils, oilseeds, grains and soybean. Its consumer products include edible oils, rice, flour and noodles in China, Indonesia, Vietnam and India. Its plantation and palm oil mills segment engages in oil palm cultivation and milling.
Wilmar has come under criticism for its exploitation of child labour and slave labour, as well as unsafe working conditions on its plantations amidst other worker mistreatment incidents. The company has also been exposed for its environmentally degrading practices, and forced displacement of poor populations, amongst other unethical behaviours.
Wilmar was ranked fourth within the global food production sector in Fortune's most admired firms list in 2026.
